questions.q: What makes a vector an eigenvector of a matrix?
options: It has length exactly 1
The matrix only stretches, shrinks or flips it, without turning it off its line
It is one of the original feature columns
The matrix turns it by 90 degrees
questions.why: An eigenvector is a direction the matrix leaves on the same line, scaled by the eigenvalue. Length 1 is just how libraries report them, not what defines them; and eigenvectors are new directions, usually blends of the original features.

questions.q: A matrix has an eigenvector v with eigenvalue −1. What does the matrix do to v?
options: Squashes it flat to zero
Leaves it completely unchanged
Halves its length
Flips it to point the opposite way, keeping its length
questions.why: A negative eigenvalue flips the direction; a size of 1 keeps the length, so Av = −v. Squashing to zero is what an eigenvalue of 0 does, and "unchanged" would be an eigenvalue of +1.

questions.q: What are the eigenvalues of A = [[3, 1], [1, 3]]?
options: 4 and 2
3 and 3
4 and −2
6 and 8
questions.why: det(A − λI) = (3 − λ)² − 1 = 0 gives 3 − λ = ±1, so λ = 4 or 2. Quick checks: they add to the trace (6) and multiply to the determinant (9 − 1 = 8). "3 and 3" reads the diagonal, which only works for diagonal matrices; 6 and 8 are the trace and determinant themselves.

questions.q: Two standardised features have correlation 0.6, so the covariance matrix is [[1, 0.6], [0.6, 1]]. What share of the variance does the first principal component explain?
questions.why: (1 − λ)² = 0.36 gives λ = 1.6 or 0.4. Share = 1.6 / (1.6 + 0.4) = **80%**. Reading the correlation (0.6) directly as the share is the tempting shortcut, but the share comes from the eigenvalue, not the correlation.

questions.q: PCA on five standardised features gives eigenvalues 4.0, 2.5, 1.0, 0.3 and 0.2. How many components do you need to keep at least 80% of the variance?
options: 5, because every feature carries information
questions.why: Total = 8.0. The first component gives 4.0/8 = 50%; adding the second gives 6.5/8 = 81.25%, past 80%. Keeping all five defeats the point of PCA; one component (50%) falls well short.

questions.q: You run PCA twice on the same data. The first run reports the top eigenvector as [0.71, 0.71], the second as [−0.71, −0.71]. What does this mean?
options: The data must have changed between the runs
The second run is a bug and the results cannot be trusted
Nothing is wrong: an eigenvector is a direction, and its sign is arbitrary
The second component has become the first
questions.why: If v is an eigenvector, so is −v, with the same eigenvalue; libraries pick a sign arbitrarily. Treating the flip as a bug is a common misreading. It only matters if you interpret the sign of a component score, so fix a sign convention before reporting.

questions.q: Each month 80% of Brand A's customers stay and 20% switch to B; 70% of B's stay and 30% switch to A. With M = [[0.8, 0.3], [0.2, 0.7]], what is Brand A's long-run market share?
options: It depends on the starting split
questions.why: The long-run share s satisfies Ms = 1 × s. Balance flows: 0.2 × A = 0.3 × B, so A : B = 3 : 2, giving A = **60%**. Check: 0.8 × 0.6 + 0.3 × 0.4 = 0.6. The starting split does not matter because the other eigenvalue (0.5) shrinks the gap every month; 80% is just A's retention rate.

questions.q: Interview: "Why should you standardise features before PCA?" Which answer is best?
options: Otherwise the feature with the largest units has the largest variance and dominates the covariance matrix, so the top component just points along it
PCA cannot run on unscaled data
Standardising guarantees the first component explains over 90% of the variance
It makes the eigenvectors come out with length 1
questions.why: Eigenvalues of the covariance matrix are variances, and variance depends on units: salary in rupees will out-vary age in years and grab the first component. PCA runs fine on raw data, which is why the mistake is easy to make. Eigenvector length is a reporting convention unrelated to scaling.
